title: The Panel
question: Where do co-reviewers of the same paper take opposite stances, how does the meta-reviewer's tone differ from the panel it summarizes, which way does the final decision err when it departs from the panel's lean, and how much ground does a panel actually cover?

figures.title: Contested ground: share of papers where reviewers took opposite stances
figures.deck: Panels split most over whether the question matters at all.

claims.statement: Reviewers split most on problem framing (38.6%) — whether the question matters — and least on robustness (16.3%), where the evidence speaks.
claims.derivation: share of papers with ≥2 official reviewers touching the object where they landed on opposite valence stances, ranked across the 12 objects (a paper counts only when at least two reviewers touched the object)

claims.statement: Across nine years of units, meta-reviewers run 13.7pp less negative and 10.5pp more positive than the panels they summarize — the judge is kinder than the prosecution.
claims.derivation: meta-reviewer unit valence mix minus official-reviewer unit valence mix, across nine years of units (PANEL.meta vs. reviewer valence shares)

figures.title: The bench: when the decision disagrees with the panel's lean
figures.deck: When the decision departs from its panel, it departs toward mercy: 919 papers lifted from below the line against 338 dropped from above it — 2.7×.

claims.statement: 919 papers were lifted from below the accept line and 338 dropped from above it — when the decision departs from its panel, it does so toward acceptance about 2.7 times as often.
claims.derivation: 919 papers accepted despite a below-line panel mean ÷ 338 rejected despite an above-line mean = 2.72, rounds to 2.7×

figures.title: The search party: what a panel covers, duplicates, and never sees
figures.deck: The panel duplicates some searches and leaves a third of the ground unwalked.

claims.statement: The average panel covers 7.95 of the twelve objects, agrees on examining only 0.83 of them, and leaves 4.05 entirely unvisited.
claims.derivation: mean count, across the 18,074 rated 2026 panels of three or four, of the 12 objects examined by ≥1 reviewer, by ≥3 reviewers (agreement), and by 0 reviewers

claims.statement: Over half of panels put three or more reviewers on empirical scope while two-thirds leave reproducibility unexamined.
claims.derivation: share of panels with ≥3 reviewers examining empirical_scope (by_object.empirical_scope[3] = 55.79%) vs. share of panels with 0 reviewers examining reproducibility (by_object.reproducibility[0] = 67.49%). The deposition previously recorded 50% and ~66.7%; corrected to the shipped values 2026-08-26. The page's prose reads these as “over half” and “two-thirds”, which both remain true.
claims.verified: claim recomputed from source island; value corrected, 2026-08-26

claims.statement: Novelty, the costliest charge on the tariff (Plate XIV), goes unexamined by every reviewer in 56% of panels.
claims.derivation: share of panels where zero reviewers examined novelty at all

caveats.text: Part of the meta-reviewer's milder tone is genre: a meta-review summarizes and justifies a decision rather than inspecting a paper, so its milder valence mix is not by itself proof of a milder mind.
caveats.scope: Fig 20a rail (meta-reviewer vs. panel valence gap)

caveats.text: The accept line is inferred from the outcomes, not published by the venue, so a paper counted as overruled may simply have been decided on information the mean does not carry — a chair's reading of the discussion, a policy on scope, a reviewer discounted. The half-point overrule margin is also a choice: recomputed at margins of 0.25, 0.75, and a full point, the ratio runs 2.4×, 3.9×, 3.9× — the direction survives any reasonable margin.
